qc_chez_roger.blurb: A big cliff in the mountains above Saint-Alphonse-Rodriguez, in Quebec's Lanaudiere region, split into lettered sectors that run right to left. The faces are steep, with crimps, overhanging arêtes and hand cracks, and sport and trad are nearly an even split; many lines mix bolts with gear, so a rack is useful. Grades run from the 5.9s to 5.12, with most between 5.10 and 5.11 and little at the easy end. Larger sectors include Helios, Promethee, Atlas and Hestia. The wall faces mostly southeast and gets plenty of sun, while deciduous forest at the base gives shade in summer. A helmet is wise, and a stick clip helps on some lines.

tn_foster_falls.blurb: A sandstone sport-climbing cliff near Jasper in southeast Tennessee, west of Chattanooga, set beside a waterfall and hiking trails. The cliff divides into around twenty sections, from slabs and dihedrals to roofed bunkers, so the character changes from wall to wall. Sport routes make up the great majority, with a few trad lines and only a handful of boulder problems. Little here is easy: the fun starts around 5.9, the bulk of the climbing is 5.10 to 5.12, and the steepest bunkers reach 5.13. Jimmywood, the Red Light District, Wall of Useless Conflict and White Wall are among the busiest sections. Climbing is possible nearly year-round, though the hottest and coldest stretches are best avoided.

co_wonderland_2.blurb: A spread-out crag area near Pine in Colorado's South Platte country, around 8,200 feet, covering roughly five square miles and more than thirty formations. Cracks, slabs and face climbs come as single and multi-pitch routes, with sport making up most of the climbing and a solid share of trad, plus a few boulder problems and a small group of mixed lines at Pleasure Dome. Grades are mostly moderate, running from the 5.5s into the 5.12s and peaking around 5.10, with a good number of easier climbs. Slab fans will feel at home. Dental Dome is one of the bigger single crags. Approaches usually take around half an hour, so it feels off the beaten path, and the area can be climbed year-round.

wv_roadside_2.blurb: A boulder-heavy sector of Coopers Rock State Forest in northern West Virginia, a short drive east of Morgantown near Interstate 68. The forest's cliffs and boulders are coarse sandstone with good friction, cracks, edges and pockets. Most climbs here are boulder problems, mostly V0 to V4 with a tail up to about V7, alongside a block of top-rope lines and a few trad routes, which makes this sector home to most of the forest's rope climbing. Cliffs are low. Sunset Wall Area is the largest sub-area, followed by Ceiling Block Area, First Set Boulders and Tendon Repair Kit Area. Spring and fall are generally the best seasons across the forest; summer is popular with forest shade, but heat, humidity and wet rock can get in the way.

bc_harrison_bluffs.blurb: South and east-facing granite bluffs in the Fraser Valley of southern British Columbia, between Agassiz and Harrison Hot Springs, at low elevation. The stone is fine-grained and grippy with plenty of pockets, giving slab, crack and steep face climbing, with a handful of multi-pitch lines. Trad is the largest share, followed by boulders and sport. Roped grades mostly run from 5.7 to 5.11 and peak around 5.10, while the boulder problems spread from V0 to V9. Sectors include The East Wall, East Boulders, West Boulders and From The Ground Up. The walls pick up morning to midday sun and the east side goes shady first. March through November is the main window, sunny winter days can work, and wet weather makes the rock slick. Crowds are small, especially midweek.
